headline: Bunker Push Bass Into Plum Gut, Jumbo Blues Right Behind
subhead: Harvest Moon tides are stacking menhaden through The Race and the Gut, and both bass and blues are committing hard on the drop.
body_markdown:
Slot and overslot stripers are getting bent rods at Plum Gut this week, and it's not subtle. Bunker schools — some the size of a basketball court, some just pods of a few hundred — are getting squeezed through the Gut and The Race on these bigger Harvest Moon tides, and the bass are shadowing them tight to bottom on the west side drop where the current stacks bait against structure. Jumbo bluefish are mixed right in, blowing up on top when the bunker get pinned, then disappearing back into the rip. We flagged this pattern last week — said the bluefish push would keep intensifying as more bait gets flushed south and east — and that's exactly what's showing up on the Gut and along the Race wall right now.

The why is straightforward. Kings Point is reading 70.9 and New London 69.4, which tells you the whole Sound is still carrying summer heat but there's a real west-to-east gradient building. That gradient is what's driving bait — bunker don't like getting squeezed into a cooling funnel, so they're pushing east and south toward the mouth, right into the two most current-charged pinch points on the whole Sound. Add in bigger moon tides moving more water faster through The Race and Plum Gut, and you've got bait getting disoriented and concentrated at exactly the structure bass and blues already know how to hunt. This is the pattern that builds through the back half of September every year, and this week it clicked.

Best window has been the last two hours of the ebb into dead low at both the Gut and the Race — that's when bunker get funneled hardest and predators pin them against the rock piles and the deeper current seams. Bucktails in the 1.5 to 2-ounce range, white or bunker-pattern, cast across the seam and let sink before a slow bottom hop, have been drawing the better bass — mid-20s to low-30-inch fish mostly, with a scattering of overslots pushing 36 to 38 inches for guys working the deeper edge on the outgoing at Orient Point. Live or chunked bunker on a fishfinder rig, 20 to 40 feet down along the west wall of the Gut, has also been putting bigger fish on the deck for the patient crowd anchoring up rather than drifting through.

Bluefish are the more consistent bite right now, and the size class has jumped. Fish in the 8 to 12-pound range are showing on topwater — poppers and stickbaits worked fast across the boils at first light — with the heaviest activity right where the current breaks off the Fishers Island side of the Gut. If you're throwing metal, a 2-ounce diamond jig retrieved through the white water gets hit almost every cast when the blues are up. The bite's not subtle when it's on, but it is tide-dependent — miss the ebb window and you're just marking bait on the sounder with nothing willing to commit.

Fluke are still worth a trip, but the clock's running out — the season closes September 30, and this warmer-than-normal water has kept fish shallower and more active later into the month than usual. Boats working the flats off Orient and the drop-offs around Plum Island have been finding keepers in the 18 to 22-inch range on white Gulp Swimming Mullets tipped with squid strips, fished on 3/4-ounce bucktails in 25 to 35 feet on the last of the incoming. It's not a wide-open bite — more a case of grinding a few solid drifts to find where the fish are holding — but the numbers have been better than a lot of guys expected for this late in the year.

Porgies are thick around the rock piles in Fishers Island Sound and off Plum Gut's western edge, and that bite hasn't slowed at all — small hooks, sandworms or clam, bounced bottom in 15 to 25 feet, still produces steady action for anyone who wants a bucket of dinner fish between tide changes. Blackfish season isn't open yet, but the water's holding warm enough that the reef structure around Fishers and Plum Gut should be loaded once the season kicks off next month — worth scouting now if you're running structure marks for October.

Looking ahead, the next several days should keep building on this pattern rather than break it. The Harvest Moon tides aren't done yet, and as long as that west-to-east thermal gradient holds, bunker are going to keep getting squeezed through the Gut and The Race, which means bass and blues should keep stacking on the same tide stages. If there's a shift coming, it's the first real cold front of the fall — when that hits, expect the fluke bite to shut down fast and the bass to start committing even harder to structure as they stage for the push south. For now, if you've only got one window this week, work the last two hours of the ebb at Plum Gut or the Race wall — that's where the bait's getting pinned, and that's where the bigger fish are showing up to eat it.
